The intersection of a pair of closed geodesics on a hyperbolic surface of genus g >= 3 can have at most 2g endpoints, with a specific, regular surface demonstrating this maximum. We show that this limit is also the minimum, and our proof relies on an understanding of isoxial Fuchsian groups, with key elements of the proof stemming from a new classification of subgroups within the Atkinsonian group, consisting of two types: reduced cyclic groups and infinitely generated subgroups.

The BFCTF experiment conducted an investigation at the BEPCII collider to detect Lepton Flavor Violation in the $\Upsilon(3S) \rightarrow e^\pm \mu^{\mp}$ process. Utilizing $70.2\times10^6$ $\Upsilon(3S)$ events, the researchers found no observable LFV signal and established 90% confidence level upper bounds on the $R_{\Upsilon(3S)}$ branching ratio ratio as high as $1.81\times10^{-7}$. This research represents the first experimental examination of LFV in the $\Upsilon(3S)$ decay.

We investigated the effect of pressure on the flat-band Kagome compounds Pd$_3$P$_2$(S$_{1-x}$Se$_x$)$_8$ ($x$ = 0, 0.25, 0.5, and 0.75) and discovered that these compounds exhibit a unique high-pressure transition to a superconducting state. Notably, our results indicate a linear relationship between the superconducting transition temperature ($T_c$) and sulfur content. This observation aligns with a previous study involving a similar compound, Pd$_3$P$_2$S$_6$, where a negative pressure coefficient for $T_c$ was observed. Furthermore, our data suggest that the superconducting transition temperature is influenced by the flat-band width, and a specific scaling behavior is demonstrated in the compound Pd$_3$P$_2$Se$_6$ below a certain pressure threshold.

We have developed a method to retrieve information from a black hole by analyzing the time-dependent evolution of its entropy in a 2-dimensional gravitational model. This approach, which does not rely on the standard decoherence concept, focuses on the time it takes for a black hole to release information, rather than losing it. Our research focuses on the theoretical framework and the time it takes for a black hole to fully release its information.

Recent advancements in neural ordinary differential equations (ODEs) have enabled
the creation of continuous representations of complex functions, particularly through
the use of neural ODE solvers that can accurately model step and continuous-time
functions. These representations are beneficial for tasks such as time series and
image analysis, as they can account for both continuous and discontinuous changes.
However, the data used to train neural ODEs is often noisy and irregular, which can
hinder the performance of neural ODEs trained on such data. To address this issue, a
new neural ODE framework is proposed that incorporates a robust neural network capable
of accurately modeling both continuous and discontinuous changes in data. The
framework is based on a novel neural ODE that can account for both continuous and
discontinuous changes in data, and is trained using a loss function that can account
for the noisy data. The proposed framework is evaluated using both simulated and
real-world data, and the results demonstrate its ability to accurately model both
continuous and discontinuous changes in data, even when the data is noisy and
irregular.

The Object Goal Navigation task demands an agent to locate a specific target object in complex indoor settings. Current approaches utilize object recognition to prioritize navigation towards the target. A recent study introduced the Object Memory Transformer, an innovative attention mechanism that combines the strengths of object recognition and visual memory to facilitate effective navigation. This attention mechanism enables the agent to accurately identify and pursue the target object, leveraging both high-level object features and low-level visual details. Experimental findings on ModelNet and Room Repairs datasets reveal that the Object Memory Transformer significantly outperforms previous methods in terms of success rate and sample efficiency.

Recent studies have shown that few-shot task adaptation with language models yields
remarkable results. Nevertheless, the current state-of-the-art systems heavily rely on
highly specialized fine-tuning techniques, resulting in suboptimal generalization and
poor performance on unseen tasks. To overcome this challenge, we propose OPT-IML, a
novel approach to instruction-based language model fine-tuning. By eliminating the
need for specific task training and constraints, OPT-IML enables seamless domain
adaptation and achieves comparable performance on standard benchmarks. Notably,
our model excels at handling out-of-domain scenarios, demonstrating substantial
gains of 8.8 and 7.4 EM scores over mT5-3B and GPT3-base on the CoRT benchmark,
respectively. The associated source code can be found on the following GitHub
repository: https://github.com/autome/OPT-IML.

This study examines the concept of Legitimate Peripheral Participation in Scratch, a children-focused programming environment that offers diverse activities for varying skill levels. We conducted a quantitative analysis of user behavior and identified numerous pathways to acquiring new skills. Our findings reveal a substantial number of users, consisting of over 10 million accounts and 16 million user-generated projects over 15 years, and our analysis of user interactions and platform features reveals a range of distinct roles for users at different skill levels. Our data highlights three distinct modes of engagement in Scratch, which correspond to the principles of Community, Planners, and Experts. Our analysis of the roles and pathways within these modes reveals a diverse array of user roles and social dynamics within the community. Our analysis further shows that users' skills and involvement develop in a diverse range of patterns, which we categorize into distinct pathways. Our study demonstrates that, consistent with the concept of LPP, users' skills and involvement progress at different rates according to their level of involvement.

Using a transcorrelated Hamiltonian, we have reformulated the electron gas in a Fermi liquid approach, and have developed an iterative perturbation theory to determine the one-particle density matrix and energy. Our approach accurately predicts the correlation energy of the electron gas for small to medium range densities, with results comparable to those from the configuration space diffusion Monte Carlo method.

We introduce a novel approach to accurately estimate the covariance matrix of a Gaussian process based on a limited spatial dataset. By incorporating location uncertainty into the covariance model, it becomes necessary to infer the covariance matrix from a probabilistic mapping of measured values to their true values. To achieve this, we derive a maximum entropy solution under a physically valid covariance constraint, formulating the problem as an optimal transportation mapping in a high-dimensional space. Due to the complexity of the resulting functional, we propose a first-order tensor product expansion of the covariance model, yielding a constrained optimization problem. By leveraging the properties of the Kullback-Leibler divergence, we demonstrate that this approximation satisfies necessary physical constraints, including positive definiteness. Numerical results on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in accurately estimating the covariance matrix, with notable improvements over existing methods.

Ensuring data privacy is a pressing concern that must be addressed in order for companies to safely release sensitive information to the public domain. This paper delves into the application of Randomized Tensor Network Decomposition (RTND) as a method for breaking down complex data into manageable parts for secure sharing. RTND leverages SVD, an established matrix decomposition technique, to decompose tensors into matrices, which are subsequently broken down into random, independent units for further analysis. RTND's reliance on SVD ensures the preservation of essential data characteristics within the decomposed matrices. RTND's efficiency is demonstrated through its ability to process large datasets across multiple computing nodes and its scalability, making it a promising solution for handling vast datasets using diverse hardware configurations. The results of this study confirm RTND's superiority over existing tensor decomposition methods in terms of accuracy, efficiency, and scalability, rendering it a promising solution for safeguarding sensitive data.

The integration of autonomous robots into human environments necessitates them to be both capable of learning from a range of experiences and to operate in harmony with human involvement. This paper introduces SafeAPT, an algorithm that enables a robot to safely learn from direct human input while exploring diverse actions and adapting to human corrections. By leveraging the benefits of both simulation-based learning and real-time feedback, SafeAPT provides a robust and efficient method for developing safe real-world robot controllers. We demonstrate the efficacy of SafeAPT through its successful application in the development of a real-world quadrotor that can seamlessly navigate a cluttered indoor environment. This quadrotor is capable of safely avoiding collisions with moving objects and can safely land on a designated area despite the unpredictability of human input. Our results confirm that SafeAPT effectively mitigates the risks associated with human input, ultimately enabling the quadrotor to safely operate in real-world settings.

The study of jet physics in radio galaxies and quasars remains a relatively underdeveloped area, despite significant progress being made in the standard model's fundamental physics in recent years. As a result, radio galaxies and quasars offer a unique opportunity to investigate jet physics in greater detail. This article aims to provide an introduction to the standard model's current status, highlighting key findings within the fields of radio galaxies and quasars. By discussing jet morphology, energetics, and particle acceleration, this review seeks to outline the standard model's current limitations and potential future research directions.

This research introduces a new statistical model for analyzing complex, non-linear time series relationships with changes over time. The model is estimated using machine learning techniques combined with simultaneous sieve analysis. Theoretical performance of the method is demonstrated under certain conditions, with further investigation into the theoretical optimal configuration through numerical simulations and an application to actual data in exchange rate dynamics.

The increasing popularity of social media has led to a rise in communication through informal, written language, which poses challenges for understanding and analysis. To address this, various studies of informal language text have employed supervised machine learning approaches, focusing on detecting the presence of offensive language within online posts. This study reviews the development and evaluation of neural models for identifying offensive language in social media text, with a primary focus on English language corpus.

The functional connectivity of brain regions can be described by graph theory, specifically edge density and centrality. We utilize a deep learning approach to discover novel functional connections between brain regions. Our model, the AutoGraph, learns to represent the brain as a graph and identify the weights of connections between these regions. We then utilize centrality to define node weights, and employ it to predict the strength of connections between brain regions. Our results indicate that AutoGraph successfully reconstructs the strength of connections between brain regions, and that its performance is directly proportional to the amount of available data. Furthermore, we find that AutoGraph accurately predicts the strength of connections between brain regions, and that these predictions are influenced by the types of tasks individuals are performing. Our study suggests that deep learning models can effectively uncover the network structure of brain regions, and that this structure is closely linked to the specific tasks individuals are attempting to complete.

This paper develops a systematic framework to analyze and optimize Nesterov's accelerated first-order optimization method using dissipativity theory from nonlinear control theory. The research establishes novel relationships between Nesterov's method and key properties of convex optimization problems. The findings enable the derivation of performance measures such as the dynamic behavior of accumulation points, the asymptotic rate of convergence, and the asymptotic gap between suboptimal solutions and the optimal solution. The research also extends to non-Euclidean settings, providing a comprehensive extension of the well-known linearized Euler scheme in dissipativity theory. The results confirm that Nesterov's method is a specific instance of this scheme, and offer insights into its behavior.

This research focuses on developing suitable boundary conditions for hyperbolic systems with varying inputs, which can be applied in multi-dimensional scenarios. A hybrid explicit-implicit framework is employed in conjunction with a matrix-free approach to solve the system efficiently, ensuring that boundary conditions are preserved. Numerical results demonstrate the effectiveness of this method in maintaining the accuracy of approximations on interior points, while also enabling the integration of complex boundary conditions that may include diffusion terms, abrupt changes, or nonlinear equations.

The solar cell's optical performance and efficiency heavily depend on its ability to capture sunlight and convert it into electrical energy. To achieve this, solar cells are typically coated with thin films that enhance their optical properties, but these films also create a problem by reducing the device's throughput and efficiency. To address this challenge, researchers have proposed a solution that involves using a 3D photonic band gap reflector to improve the device's absorption capabilities, especially in thin films. By using this technology, it is possible to increase the device's efficiency to a level comparable to thicker and more efficient solar cells, even when using extremely thin films.

This paper introduces credVal-Net, a novel, transparent, and reliable inference method for machine reasoning under uncertainty. CredVal-Net builds upon the credVal framework, which assigns precise meanings to uncertain natural language arguments, thereby distinguishing certain, probable, possible, and uncertain conclusions. The credVal framework is then integrated with neural networks to create credVal-Net, which can be utilized for a variety of applications, such as evaluating the credibility of evidence, classifying arguments, and drawing inferences. The proposed model is compared to other cutting-edge argument mining systems and exhibits superior performance, according to results obtained from experiments conducted on the Argumentation Mining Shared Task dataset.

Personalized recommendation systems are widely utilized in e-commerce and search engines, and their performance can be significantly enhanced by incorporating nearest-neighbor search techniques. However, traditional metric learning methods rely on fixed margins, which fail to adapt to the complexities of user preference patterns, and consequently, lead to suboptimal results. To address this issue, we propose an innovative method that dynamically adjusts margins through probabilistic analysis and adaptive learning processes. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated using an expectation-maximization algorithm, which is then applied to a real-world dataset. Experimental results reveal that our method not only outperforms traditional metric learning methods but also achieves higher accuracy and faster convergence rates.

The eternally non-Markovian Pauli channel serves as a simple yet highly relevant 
example to investigate the non-unital channel's distinguishing features. 
Initially, we establish a condition for a unital channel to also be non-unital, 
utilizing a specific operator. Subsequently, we demonstrate that this operator 
plays a crucial role in the eternally non-Markovian Pauli channel, essentially 
capturing its underlying dynamics. Furthermore, we show that this operator enables 
the creation of non-trivial, non-unital channels on finite Hilbert spaces, 
including those that are bijective. Finally, we examine the connection between 
non-unital and non-Markovian channels and discuss their implications for quantum 
information processing.

Recent advances in machine learning have led to the development of sophisticated classifiers, enabling the construction of decision trees through counterfactual reasoning. This approach involves identifying key attributes and their potential alternatives, thereby facilitating a more informed decision-making process. By analyzing different scenarios, such as the most critical attribute or its most plausible substitute, the trained model can effectively assess complex situations. To further enhance the accuracy of these classifiers, an active learning mechanism is proposed, which selectively identifies and optimizes the most effective counterfactual attributes. Experimental results demonstrate that this counterfactual-based approach significantly outperforms traditional decision trees in terms of classification accuracy.

Creating a semantic map of an environment involves converting raw data from sensors into a meaningful representation that can be used for navigation. To achieve this, prior knowledge of the setting can be incorporated, making it easier to generate more accurate maps. In our research, we developed RoSmEEry - an open-source, Gazebo-based simulation platform designed for evaluating and fine-tuning semantic mapping algorithms. RoSmEEry comes with pre-built Gazebo scenes based on real-world environments, including a robotic warehouse and a home setting. The platform also includes a range of pre-trained machine learning models for object detection and category classification. By using these models within the simulation, we can efficiently simulate the behavior of the semantic mapping pipeline, allowing for faster testing and evaluation of the system. Our results demonstrate the potential of RoSmEEry to quickly assess and compare the performance of different semantic mapping algorithms.

Rikudo is a modified Tic-Tac-Toe variant where each turn can place multiple X's on a single grid location, with the goal of being the first to attain $|\bullet| + |X| + |o| + 1$ stones. Contrary to its straightforward rules, determining the winner in Rikudo appears to be a computationally complex task. However, it can be confirmed that the game's winner can be identified in polynomial time. Nonetheless, the primary question at hand revolves around finding the winning strategy for Rikudo, a challenge that we prove to be computationally expensive by demonstrating its NP-completeness.

The classic OT problem, framed as a linear programming issue, poses computational obstacles when dealing with extensive, high-resolution input data. The advent of optimal transport has led to its application in diverse fields such as biology, computer science, and physics, necessitating efficient solutions for large-scale problems. This guide offers an overview of OT methods, focusing on those employing Sinkhorn method alternatives for approximately solving the OT problem in a fully discrete setting, and also discussing algorithms for computing discrete OT functions and gradients.

This work explores the connection between Hecke groups and Ramanujan's modular equations for signatures 2, 3, and 4. Specifically, we establish that the modular equations form polynomial automorphisms of the ring of integers in the Hilbert class field, and we provide polynomial expressions describing these automorphisms. Our method involves using modular forms and the generalized Umfassende Tatzelwurf theorem.

The Keck ESI spectrograph has been utilized to obtain high-resolution redshift measurements and velocity dispersions of 11 lensing galaxies in eight quasar systems that are gravitationally lensed. These observations were made over a period of more than ten years, with data collected during periods of both photometric and non-photometric conditions. The resulting velocity dispersion measurements were found to be in agreement with previous observations, with one exception, where the discrepancy may be attributed to a non-uniform distribution of stars in one of the galaxies. The high-quality data allowed for the generation of accurate lens models for each system, with one system yielding a hitherto unseen image, previously missed by the Hubble Space Telescope. The findings also enabled a detailed investigation of the mass distribution of one system, with the aid of previously obtained data. The data further allowed for the derivation of the time delay of one system, with the resulting value being in agreement with previous estimates.

This work explores the $q$-fractional differential equations on time scales when subjected to nonhomogeneous boundary conditions. A class of $q$-fractional difference equations is developed to approximate the solution, along with an examination of the convergence between the discrete and analytical solutions. Error analysis for the approximate solution's error bounds is conducted, demonstrating linear convergence. Numerical examples are presented to validate the proposed method.

The theoretical model of the phonon Hall effect, which was introduced by Lu et al., can be explained and understood through the lens of topological phonons. A precise calculation, which is based on the topological invariant, shows that the phonon Hall conductivity does not adhere to the standard linear relationship expected from a classical Hall effect, but instead follows a quadratic pattern. Moreover, this calculation also indicates that the phonon Hall effect can exhibit non-monotonic behavior, which is in line with the predictions made using the Boltzmann approach.

A new Raman imaging approach, called Widespread Shifted Excitation Raman Imaging (WSRI), is inspired by NRSI. In this study, we developed a WSRI protocol that can capture Raman spectra of numerous points in a large area. The Nod and Shuffle technique was used to collect Raman spectra of the same area at two different wavelengths and then remove the fluorescence background. The resulting WSR spectra showed the Raman signal enhancements. The WSR imaging method was then applied to detect cancer cells in a breast tissue sample. The results indicated that the WSR imaging method successfully identified cancer cells in a complex biological system.

This study investigates matrix analogues of Fejér and Levin-Stečkin inequalities for matrix polynomials. Specifically, it examines and addresses several issues related to these inequalities in the context of matrix polynomials, including establishment, sharpness, characterization through spectral conditions, and analysis of convergence. Notably, this research leads to new findings on the rate of convergence of Lebesgue integrals comprising eigenvalues of a given matrix, which may have practical applications.

We investigate the average null energy condition for black holes that shrink as they emit, focusing specifically on the dynamics within the horizon where the energy density is unbounded and the condition is unfulfilled. Our findings indicate that the average null energy density in relation to time doesn't adhere to the condition, but interestingly, a precise upper limit can be established based on scalar curvature. Notably, this limit exhibits a direct correlation with time, suggesting that black holes with larger masses tend to evade the condition for a longer period.

This dissertation investigates the conformal Field Theories (CFTs) from a perspective that combines theoretical foundations and practical applications. Initially, we delve into the theoretical underpinnings of CFTs, examining two key models based on conformal groups - the conformal Gross-Neveu model and the O(N)-vector model. The model based on conformal group Cn(1,1) is utilized to calculate the cross-sections of graviton scattering at leading orders in graviton fields and low-energy limits. Furthermore, we explore the connection between a specific CFT, the N-state Potts model, and its associated model based on the cyclic group. This relationship is utilized to calculate the cross-sections of boson scattering. The relationship between the two models is further expanded to calculate the four-point functions of relevant operators. Ultimately, we examine the critical properties of a model based on the SU(2) group, specifically the SU(2) Heisenberg model, at low-energy limits.

To address the pressing security issues in Industrial Control Systems (ICSs), a comprehensive Cybersecurity Testbed Maturity Model (CTM2) has been proposed. This model enables users to create and maintain a large-scale ICS testbed, facilitating research and development in ICS security. A testbed's construction is a complex process, and our model aims to guide users every step of the way. This proof-of-concept study focuses on constructing an ICS testbed for simulating real-world scenarios. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of CTM2 in assisting researchers in this endeavor.

In complex environments, multi-agent reinforcement learning is a key strategy for achieving coordinated behavior. However, finding an optimal solution is challenging due to the need to balance cooperation and self-interest. To overcome this issue, we introduce a new approach for representing the value function in MARL. By focusing on a subset of states, we can approximate the optimal policy and enhance efficiency. The proposed method is based on a greedy algorithm and incorporates a boundary state selection algorithm, reducing the computational time required for value function estimation. Experimental results, conducted in a realistic autonomous vehicle scenario, demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, outperforming existing methods in terms of efficiency and overall performance.

Biases embedded in language models pose a threat to fair machine learning practices. Research has uncovered biases that models learn from their training data, which can perpetuate harmful attitudes. Existing studies have primarily focused on biases related to race, gender, and sexuality. This paper investigates whether pre-trained language models also acquire stereotypical biases, which affect how actions are associated with characteristics like age, gender, racial or ethnic background, or occupation. We assess the extent to which these biases are reflected in 12 prominent language models, including BERT, GPT, XLNet, GPT3, RoBERTa, and DistilBERT, using a new dataset called StereoSet that we developed. StereoSet is a collection of 1,600 questions that test for stereotypical biases, which we created by combining a reference list of action-term pairs with a set of characteristics. StereoSet is the first resource of its kind to measure such biases in language models. We used StereoSet to evaluate the models' ability to make predictions based on characteristics, which we measured using the Brier score. Our results show that all the models we tested learned strong biases, which often align with human biases.

Optimizing Remote Electrical Tilt (RET) is crucial for improving the performance of 5G new radio (NR) connections. Current methods for optimizing RET rely on continuous approximation, which isn't very accurate. To address this issue, we've developed an off-policy learning technique that doesn't rely on this inaccurate approximation, allowing for more precise results. To implement this method, we've created a simulated environment that can learn from random exploration. Through experiments, we've shown that our method significantly outperforms traditional methods, with considerable differences in policy outcomes between the two approaches. Furthermore, we've found that off-policy learning allows for more efficient learning and better generalization to different network conditions.

A multi-variable analysis has been conducted on $B^{0} \rightarrow h^{+}h^{-}$ decays using LHCb data, offering the most comprehensive and precise estimate yet of the CKM angle $\gamma$ within the Standard Model framework. The analysis combines results from $B^{0} \rightarrow \phi K^{*}(892)\to K^{+}K^{-}K^{+}K^{-}$, $B^{0} \to (\pi^{+}\pi^{-})K^{+}K^{-}$, and $B^{0} \to (\pi^{+}\pi^{-})(\pi^{+}\pi^{-})K^{+}K^{-}$ decays. The analysis yields a CKM angle $\gamma$ value of $(85.0^{+3.1}_{-3.8})^{\circ}$, which is in line with Standard Model predictions.

Several properties of complex ellipsoids among convex bodies in n-space are examined. Specifically, both their section properties and those of their polar counterparts are investigated in relation to other convex bodies. Additionally, our findings regarding the section properties of complex ellipsoids align with those of real ellipsoids, whereas we establish that, contrary to expectation, complex symmetry is not a characteristic of complex ellipsoids; rather, we define and study a more nuanced concept, namely, complex concave symmetry, for these shapes.

Recent studies on personal data trading within data markets have yielded significant findings. This research seeks to explore an alternative approach, where individuals can voluntarily sell data on an open market. A novel platform, called Polaris, was developed to facilitate this concept. Conducting focus groups and surveys with 75 participants, we gathered insights into their perceptions, concerns, and experiences when using popular apps (Instagram, Facebook, WhatsApp, and Snapchat). Our research identified three key takeaways: first, individuals are willing to monetize their data, albeit with caution; second, they prefer data markets over traditional end-to-end encryption; and third, education plays a crucial role in increasing data trading participation. These discoveries have significant implications for the future of personal data markets.

A new approach to detect FTN signaling called DLSD uses deep learning and is more efficient than traditional list sphere decoding. DLSNDD's architecture allows it to be trained specifically for each signaling rate, which increases its accuracy. It achieves this by converting the soft decisions into binary values, utilizing a multi-label problem formulation and matrix-to-vector operations. The DLSNDD's performance was evaluated through numerical simulations and was compared to traditional LS and two previous DLSD versions. The results show that the DLSNDD achieves a significant decrease in computational complexity of 3.5 times for 8-PSK modulation and a bit rate of 1.25 times Nyquist at a 0.5 dB performance loss, compared to traditional LS.

This study introduces order topology and Frink ideal topology to arbitrary effect algebras. It is proven that these topologies are compact, 0-based, and Hausdorff, and the closure of the set that includes only 0 is the entire space. Furthermore, the topology is derived using a specific measure of the size of the chains within the effect algebra, and it is shown that this topological space's compactness is equivalent to the property that each finite subset has a supremum. Additionally, the discussion of the order topology's properties leads to the conclusion that the effect algebra's internal capacity is countable. It is also demonstrated that the Frink ideal topology is a compact Hausdorff topological space, and every element in the effect algebra is the union of all its smallest Frink ideals.

Recent advancements in deep learning models have achieved exceptional performance across numerous domains, yet these models often exhibit overconfidence in their predictions, particularly when faced with minor alterations to the input data. To mitigate this issue, we introduce SaliencyMix, a data augmentation technique that inverts the typical approach by selectively replacing input pixels with random values. Instead of relying on random changes, SaliencyMix identifies and modifies the pixels most influential for each sample, as indicated by the saliency maps. By doing so, SaliencyMix promotes the model to focus on the most critical features, leading to improved robustness and performance. Comprehensive experiments on ImageNet-1K, ImageNet-19, CIFAR-10/100, and SVHN demonstrate that SaliencyMix achieves competitive results with established data augmentation methods.

The infinite-dimensional Iwahori--Hecke algebras $\mathcal{H}_\infty^q(\mathfrak{g})$ are defined by defining a family of algebras parameterized by $q$, where $q$ ranges from $0$ to $1$. These algebras are generated by specific elements, referred to as $\kappa$ and $\rho$, and are defined over the algebra $\mathfrak{U}(\mathfrak{g})$ known as the universal enveloping algebra. In a recent paper, the author provided a proof that the dual of the algebra $\mathcal{H}_\infty^1(\mathfrak{sl_2})$ is isomorphic to the direct sum of the center of the algebra and the augmentation ideal. The author now aims to extend this result to the general case of the algebra $\mathcal{H}_\infty^q(\mathfrak{g})$. In this paper, the author provides a proof of the dual isomorphism for the algebras $\mathcal{H}_\infty^q(\mathfrak{g})$ and its dual for the specific case of $q=1$, and also provides a detailed description of the simple $\mathcal{H}^q(\mathfrak{g})$-modules. The author's work is a generalization of the findings in the previous paper written by the same author

A new cosmic method is proposed for measuring the galactic anisotropy intrinsic to each galaxy by combining it with the cosmic shear effect. This approach is crucial for analyzing the gravitational influence of galaxies on a large scale, and its accuracy relies on the precise tracking of galaxy shapes and orientations. We have developed a method to improve the intrinsic galaxy shape measurement and found that the intrinsic galaxy anisotropy can be accurately measured by combining it with the cosmic shear effect. This method is used to test alternative gravity theories, and our results show that the intrinsic galaxy shape measurement and the cosmic shear effect work together to constrain modified Horndeski gravity on a large scale. This method is more effective than traditional techniques that measure the gravitational influence of galaxies and relies on the accurate tracking of galaxy shapes and orientations.

We have conducted in-depth numerical simulations of the collective behavior of flexible, non-rigid spheres in a fluid environment, both in terms of their inherent mechanics and their interaction with the surrounding fluid. Through manipulation of key parameters such as the stiffness and the rest state length of the spheres, we observed a range of distinct behaviors, including a solid-like phase characterized by strong cohesion, a gas-like phase where particles freely diffuse, and various forms of fluid-like and glass-like phases. Notably, we observed a glass-like phase featuring a high level of rigidity and a significant degree of diffusive slowing down, which was previously unreported in literature on soft, deformable particles. Moreover, our study revealed that the glass-like phase exhibits a divergent and non-conventional stress response, which is distinct from the behavior typically observed in solid-like phases formed by thermal fluctuations. Our findings have implications for understanding the rheological properties of dense, soft-matter systems, including those encountered in various industrial applications, such as the processing of soft polymers and biocompatible biomimetic materials.

The melting behavior of gold nanoparticles has been studied using molecular dynamics simulations, examining solid-liquid phase transitions in high-resolution structures of nanoparticles with diameters between 1.5 nm and 12.1 nm. To facilitate data-driven simulations, machine learning models were created to predict melting points and lattice structures based on particle size. To enhance simulation efficiency, an adaptive integration method is proposed that leverages machine learning to account for inaccuracies in particle lattice configurations. The results show that larger nanoparticles with diameters over 1.3 nm have a melting point consistent with experimental observations, whereas smaller nanoparticles exhibit a first-order melting transition contrary to expected behavior. The study also reveals that melting points are sensitive to lattice orientation and that melting is not a uniform process in small nanoparticles. The findings suggest that adaptive integration can significantly reduce computational costs associated with certain simulations.

This is the beginning of a series focused on generalized Krasnosel'skii maps and their applications to multiparameter problems, specifically generalizations of well-known Theorems on the Separation and Bifurcation. This work builds upon and broadens the scope of previous research, as outlined in the study by Chen et al. (2014) in the Journal of Functional Analysis. The paper establishes abstract findings that serve as the foundation for subsequent investigations in bifurcation theory, multi-parameter Krasnosel'skii maps, and topological degree theory.

The model presented in this study is an extension of the $SU(5)$ Grand Unified Theory, where all the unified theory's constraints, including flavor and renormalization group equivalence, are met within a single framework, dubbed the Tetrahedron of Flavors. By incorporating these constraints, the equivalent of a $U(2)$ symmetry emerges, where all the quark masses and couplings align with data, including the recent $b$-anomalies. Moreover, the Higgs mass, Yukawa couplings, and QCD parameters are accurately predicted, while the Higgs and other particles' decay rates are naturally suppressed, consistent with experimental findings. Additionally, the model resolves the neutron $g-2$ anomaly and predicts the masses of various hadrons with remarkable precision.

We derive alternative approaches for (h;q)-Genocchi numbers and polynomials with varying weights alpha. The findings are represented using the p-adic q-integral on Zp. Subsequently, we obtain and discuss multiple identity conclusions from our derived formulae, which include the inclusion of two distinct cases.

In cases where a patient receives multiple treatments over time, traditional methods used in randomized trials are often inadequate. This paper presents an approach that leverages reinforcement learning to estimate the long-term effects of sequential treatments. The researchers propose policy evaluation algorithms based on RL to compare different treatment strategies. The validity of the resulting analysis in clinical data is ensured by applying the causal framework of "dynamic treatment regimes." The study also establishes a connection between the proposed RL methods and established statistical techniques in this field. The researchers examine the performance of the RL methods in policy evaluation and compare them to a popular matching algorithm.

To counteract recall bias in case-control studies, researchers use an auxiliary study with a small case series, assessing the recall of past exposures in cases and controls. However, these auxiliary studies are often too small to be independently published, raising questions about their reliability. We developed an auxiliary study simulation model to evaluate the recall bias correction process. In our model, we analyzed how cases and controls recall behavior, as well as how past exposures influence these behaviors, to determine past exposure distributions. We then used these distributions to correct for recall bias in our case-control study, comparing the outcomes to those from the traditional auxiliary study. Our results show that our method provides consistent risk estimates for both the auxiliary and case-control studies. In contrast, the traditional method only provides consistent risk estimates for the case-control study.

Generative autoencoders, a type of model that combines elements of generative and unsupervised models, enables the reconstruction of high-dimensional data while capturing its underlying structure. These models have been instrumental in various data analysis tasks, such as dimensionality reduction and change detection. Despite their benefits, training generative autoencoders is a complex challenge, as traditional methods, which involve approximating latent variables, can be unreliable and may lead to biased estimates. In this study, we propose a novel approach to train exact maximum likelihood generative autoencoders using invertible layers, thereby resolving the estimation difficulties associated with approximate maximum likelihood methods. Our experiments demonstrate the efficacy of this method on real-world datasets, showcasing its potential to revolutionize generative model training across multiple domains.

The Smart City concept leverages data-driven decision making, but
underutilizes existing data resources. Extracting valuable insights requires more
than basic statistical summaries. A Smart City data management system should
be able to uncover complex relationships, predict future trends, and
streamline decision making, ultimately enhancing the quality of life for its
citizens. This work proposes an advanced data mining technique that goes beyond
traditional methods by identifying correlated patterns in smart city data.
Our approach involves visualizing high-order patterns in sensor readings to
uncover meaningful relationships. Our system has been successfully tested on realworld data collected from smart city sensors, demonstrating its ability to
discover and analyze complex smart data patterns.

This work explores the development of geometric multigrid preconditioners for lower-order Hybrid Discontinuous Galerkin finite element methods applied to reaction-diffusion equations and generalized Stokes equations in 2D and 3D. We establish theoretical proof for the convergence rate of the multigrid method and show that it can achieve a maximum of 2 and nearly optimal convergence rates of 4 for the mentioned equations. We also present numerical evidence supporting the effectiveness and efficiency of the multigrid preconditioners.

A new sensitivity analysis framework has been developed to assess the reliability of missing data models in regression analysis. This approach, based on a Bayesian methodology, evaluates the uncertainty of estimated relationships by considering various scenarios of missingness and data-outlier distributions. Through a case study, we examine how different models and data-outlier distributions impact the findings of a previous study, which identified an association between a metal worker's exposure to arsenic and esophageal cancer. Our results show that the results are sensitive to the data-outlier distribution used, and using a Bayesian model, we find that the association is unlikely to be affected by the presence of data-outliers. This framework has been released as an R package to facilitate the application of Bayesian sensitivity analysis in missing data models.

In crossover trials with missing gene expression data, a multivariate mixed-effects model appears to be the most suitable approach. Traditional maximum likelihood estimators, used to obtain parameter estimates for the fixed effects and the variance of the random effects, can be inaccurate when there are missing observations. To overcome this limitation, a two-stage approach is proposed, incorporating a multiple imputation strategy based on the multivariate mixed-effects model. Consequently, a likelihood-based estimator is developed to estimate the fixed effects, and the resulting estimates are found to have asymptotically normal distributions, allowing for accurate inference in small samples. To demonstrate the proposed method's efficacy, a simulation study is conducted to evaluate its performance. Furthermore, a data analysis case study is presented to highlight the proposed method's practical application.

This study's primary goal is to define and investigate the concept of weakly monoidal categories, which is distinct from traditional monoidal categories.  We establish the relationship between weakly monoidal categories and Stasheff A(n)-cohomology, leveraging MacLane's initial ideas on cohomology theories for category variations.  Furthermore, we delve into the A(n)-cohomology of building a weak monoidal category and explore the underlying properties of its associahedra.  Building upon this foundation, we introduce the concept of Stasheff A(∞)-algebras and examine how they correspond to weak monoidal categories.  Ultimately, we explore potential areas of research for weakly monoidal categories and related theories.

DRAM has become an essential component in modern computer systems, accounting for the majority of memory access time and energy consumption.  In order to improve performance, various optimization techniques have been developed, such as utilizing multiple memory banks and implementing interleaving.  In addition, custom memory functions such as cache-friendly data structures can also be created.  In an attempt to provide a flexible platform for these custom functions, several approaches have been introduced, including in-memory processing units and custom memory technologies.  In an effort to bridge the gap between these approaches, a new system called CODIC has been developed.  CODIC allows software to control memory functions in real-time, similar to how a CPU controls the execution of instructions.  By utilizing a new memory abstraction layer, CODIC enables memory functions to be controlled and optimized.  In order to implement CODIC, a new memory architecture is introduced, which includes a new memory controller and a new memory organization. This research paper series delves into the role of functional programming in managing and orchestrating virtual network resources. Focusing on the challenges posed by the Network Functions Virtualization paradigm, the study examines the role of functional programming in addressing these issues. Having covered the fundamental concepts and issues related to FNPs and their application in resource management and orchestration through the first paper, this paper explores the role of functional programming in network evolution and design. It highlights the potential of functional programming to facilitate innovation and progress in various fields, including virtualization, network architecture, and AI-driven network systems.

This research evaluates the effectiveness of single-shot quantum gate operations within a toric code framework, with a focus on comparing the performance of different gate types, including multi-qubit gates, at varying error rates. Our investigation found that, under real-world error conditions, the average lifespan of a stored quantum bit is significantly influenced by the specific type of gate utilized. Specifically, we observed that, at a physical error rate of 0.5%, the average lifetime with a high error rate X-type gate is approximately 42 times shorter than a Clifford gate. Conversely, utilizing a phase-flip error type resulted in a lifespan nearly 20 times shorter. Our analysis also revealed that, when single-shot error correction is employed, most gates fail within a single application, whereas a subset of gates, including those with higher entanglement levels, demonstrated improved performance.

The OPUS system enables secure job submissions to infiniband clusters via GRIDSS's Secure Job Submission Protocol. Additionally, it supports secure data transfer to and from GridPHS, a physics data repository, leveraging the PHP Storage Protocol. By doing so, it executes tasks requiring CPU, data processing, and data sharing concurrently.

Computer simulations have become a valuable resource for teaching students,
enabling them to gain practical experience in intricate fields such as wireless networks.
However, traditional simulations that mirror real-world data may lead students to feel disconnected from the learning process.
To address this, our research presents an innovative digital game-based platform designed to educate students about wireless networks.
The platform allows students to engage in network simulations from a fresh perspective, fostering a more immersive and enjoyable learning environment.

The combination of ozone and molecular oxygen is a reliable indicator of the presence of oxygen in an atmosphere, provided that there is no oxygen substitute, and it is often used in the search for bioindicators on exoplanets. However, it's crucial to know whether the O2-O3 relationship remains constant across different atmospheric compositions. We have used atmospheric modeling to study how varying CO, N2, and H2 levels affect the O2-O3 relationship in low-O2, intermediate, and high-O2 regimes. We found that the O2-O3 slope is sensitive to the concentration of N2 and H2, decreasing as their levels increase. This sensitivity is more pronounced in low-O2 regimes and less pronounced in high-O2 regimes. We also discovered that the O2 upper limit is influenced by the presence of N2 and H2, while the O3 lower limit is unaffected. We used a simple model to explain the impact of N2 and H2 on the O2-O3 slope, attributing it to the equilibrium between oxygen sources and sinks. We found that the O2 upper limit is more susceptible to the concentration of N2 and H2, while the O3 lower limit is more resistant. This study highlights the importance of considering atmospheric composition when using the O2-O3 relation to search for bioindicators on exoplanets.

The quantum Hall effect's robustness has been attributed to equilibrium properties of Hall conductance, yet some studies suggest that non-equilibrium effects could still lead to robust outcomes. We investigate this by analyzing the Hofstadter model under non-equilibrium conditions, focusing on the quantum Hall effect along the z-axis. We find that non-equilibrium surface currents are surprisingly stable, even without the topological equivalence principle, and are not influenced by the model's periodicity parameter. This resilience is linked to the interplay of equilibrium Hall conductance and a chiral edge current that arises from the lattice's geometry. We also confirm that these non-equilibrium surface currents can be observed in optical analogues of quantum Hall systems.

Recent advancements in multilingual neural machine translation (NMT) have led to increased focus on fine-tuning models for specialized domains such as medicine. However, the effectiveness of these models in real-world applications remains unclear. In this study, we investigate the advantages and limitations of using pre-trained multilingual NMT models that require minimal additional training for specific medical domains. We evaluate our approach by comparing the performance of three methods: (1) translating medical text directly using a general multilingual model, (2) refining the general model with a limited amount of domain-specific data, and (3) refining the general model with a large dataset from a similar domain. Our results show that refining the general model with a small amount of domain-specific data yields the best results, outperforming the other approaches. This approach also offers practical advantages, including faster training times and reduced data requirements.

A theoretical study using the perturbation method has been conducted to analyze the influence of non-thermal electrons, positively charged dust, and the temperature of the ion fluid on slow, modified-ion-acoustic waves in plasmas with cold, negatively charged electrons and positive ions. The study found that the properties of these waves, such as their speed and thickness, are significantly affected by the temperature of the ion fluid and the density of positively charged dust. The study further investigated how the density of positively charged dust influences the formation of different types of waves, and found that it plays a crucial role in the formation of modified-ion-acoustic shock waves. The study also found that the formation of these waves is highly dependent on the range of parameters used, and that the formation of modified-ion-acoustic solitary shock waves is possible under certain conditions. The study's findings have implications for the understanding of non-linear wave dynamics in space and the formation of dust-acoustic modulations and shock waves in the lower atmosphere of the Sun and in the magnetosphere of Saturn.

The primary challenge in natural language processing tasks is creating effective
representations for text. A recent approach to this issue, denoted as dense retrieval,
involves using embeddings that enable the semantic distance between text to be
calculated through the L2 distance. This method excels in efficiency and performance
but has a limitation in that it necessitates the availability of labeled data for the
task at hand. To address this, unsupervised approaches have emerged, focusing on
generating sentence representations through context-aware modeling. This work
introduces an unsupervised method for pre-training language models that can handle
multiple languages and is designed for dense retrieval, leveraging a contrastive loss
function. Our model incorporates a sentence encoder that generates sentence
representations by processing the sentence along with its context. This approach
demonstrates superior performance in terms of efficiency and accuracy, achieving new
state-of-the-art results on a range of benchmarks, including the MS MARCO dataset.

Multimodal learning, which combines various types of data to make more accurate inferences, is hindered by the issue of modality imbalance. This imbalance, caused by differences in data distribution, significantly affects the learning process. Although current methods address the imbalance issue in single-modal systems, it remains unsolved in multimodal learning scenarios. In this research, a novel approach called Prototypical Modal Rebalance is proposed to tackle this problem. This method, which incorporates the concept of prototypical networks, can model high-level representations using only a few samples, and is capable of handling class imbalances. The approach involves creating a prototypical set for each modality to reflect the class distribution, and a reweighting mechanism to mitigate the effect of modality imbalance. Furthermore, a dynamic modality selection mechanism is developed to choose the most relevant modality for a specific task, and a loss function that encourages diversity among selected modalities to improve overall performance. The proposed method demonstrates superior results in multimodal classification tasks and is capable of balancing modality distributions, as demonstrated through experiments on object recognition, scene recognition, and natural language processing tasks.

Using the Wigner function formalism, the Vlasov equation is generalized to incorporate both scalar and vector gravitational forces. The Vlasov equation with a vector interaction is derived as a first-order approximation and the Vlasov equation with both scalar and vector gravitational forces are treated as second-order approximations. The influence of the vector interaction on the gravitational wave production and the impact of both scalar and vector gravitational forces on gravitational wave dispersion are examined in detail. The findings reveal that the Vlasov equation with scalar and vector gravitational forces can be represented by a dispersion relation that includes 16 complex poles. The analysis of the poles indicates that the vector interaction has a more significant impact on the gravitational wave production than the scalar interaction, particularly at low frequencies. The influence of the vector interaction on the gravitational wave production is substantial and increases as the frequency decreases. The findings also show that the Vlasov equation with scalar and vector gravitational forces can be used to derive a dispersion relation that includes 16 complex poles. This study explores the application of a hybrid model using a tensor-train network for spoken command recognition, combining a tensor-train network-based acoustic model with a linear classifier utilizing Mel-frequency cepstral coefficient features. Experimental results indicate that the proposed hybrid model yields comparable performance to state-of-the-art models when utilizing the same network structure, yet it requires significantly fewer parameters.

The process of simulating open quantum dynamics is significantly influenced by the choice of representation. In this study, the Pauli and Jordan-Schwinger transformations are employed to transform the Lindblad master equation in an interacting qubit-anharmonic-oscillator framework. By expressing this equation in various bases, the optimal control problem for non-Markovian quantum dynamics is investigated and numerical strategies for optimal control are presented. Our results show that the Jordan-Schwinger representation yields a well-posed optimization problem, whereas the Pauli representation does not, due to the presence of a non-smooth term. Utilizing the Schrödinger equation, the trajectories obtained from both representations are confirmed to be consistent.

Enhancing light absorption in thin-film solar cells can be achieved through
metal-nanoparticle scattering, particularly when the nanoparticles are designed
to resonate with visible light frequencies. Our investigation focuses on the
impact of aluminum nanoparticle shape on direct and indirect optical absorption
in silicon thin-film solar cells. By employing finite-difference time-domain methods,
we examined how different shapes of aluminum nanoparticles, including spheres, ellipsoids,
and pyramidal shapes, affect optical absorption in the visible and ultraviolet
spectral range. Our findings indicate that aluminum nanoparticles in the form of
pyramids significantly increase optical absorption, particularly in the visible
region of the spectrum. Moreover, the pyramidal shape leads to a substantial boost
in direct and indirect optical absorption, with a notable increase of up to 43% in the
400-550 nm wavelength range. This enhancement is attributed to the enhanced light
scattering capabilities of pyramidal-shaped aluminum nanoparticles.

The study of developing programming languages to represent the exact computational power of polynomial time (PTIME) has significant theoretical value. This investigation focuses on language design capable of representing PTIME using only non-unary, non-negation-branching logic, without counting constructs, yet incorporating a choice operator. It is proposed that the logic, dubbed $\mathsf{C}^2\mathbf{N}$, can be used to represent PTIME, with a proposed proof by reduction to a modified logic, $\mathbf{N}^2\mathbf{N}$. This reduction is a key challenge, with existing proofs for the lower bound, including the relationship with $\mathbf{N}^2\mathbf{N}$, to be examined in depth.

LSTM networks have become a leading deep learning method for video recognition tasks, but implementing them on resource-constrained hardware is challenging due to their complex design. To address this issue, we have developed a novel, low-cost hardware accelerator for video recognition that uses hierarchical Tucker tensor decomposition to reduce the model's size and minimize the required memory. Our accelerator features a high-performance processing element that enables fast matrix multiplication, and a dataflow design that optimizes memory access and minimizes control overhead. We have also developed a training framework that allows for efficient learning of high-order tensors, and have used it to develop a tensor decomposition method that takes advantage of the model's sparsity. Experimental results show that our approach outperforms other state-of-the-art tensor-based methods in terms of accuracy, and that it achieves significant reductions in memory usage and computational overhead.

The MAVLink protocol, used by numerous drones and UAVs, is vulnerable to a well-known attack known as the replay attack, taking advantage of its lack of security measures. In this research, a new security protocol based on the TLS framework is developed to safeguard the MAVLink protocol and its associated applications. A potential solution to the memory constraints of UAVs is proposed, and we introduce a lightweight cryptographic algorithm, utilizing SHA-256 and RSA-1024, to address these limitations. Our implementation, MAVSec, is evaluated on Ardupilot UAVs, and we assess its effectiveness in protecting against the well-documented replay attack, and touch upon potential future research paths.

Emulating various network topologies on demand is crucial for networking research and teaching. Traditional network simulators have limitations when it comes to handling large-scale, decentralized networks with dynamic connections. To address this, we developed Kollaps, a decentralized, dynamic topology emulation system. Kollaps enables the creation and sharing of topology descriptions, the establishment of dynamic linkages between nodes, and the automatic configuration of participating hosts. This leads to the formation of virtual networks with the topology specified by Kollaps, where the hosts operate in a peer-to-peer manner, forwarding packets and maintaining connectivity. 

Kollaps facilitates the creation and management of virtual networks with various network types, including graphs, graphs with time-based elements, software-defined networks, and virtual networks with time-based elements. The system also allows for the dynamic establishment of linkages between nodes, enabling research on complex, scaleless, and dynamic networks. 

Kollaps is an open-source, community-driven project, with the source code available on GitHub. The project's documentation is publicly accessible, and its services are available for free, making it an excellent choice for researchers and professionals.

We provide a detailed expansion of the Newman-Penrose transformation from twistor space to spin cohomology, exploring its underlying rationale and scope. The method relies on the representation of solutions to the twistor equation as the fibers of a specific projective bundle over complex projective space, where finite holonomy groups arise at each fiber. This framework allows for the systematic extension of the Newman-Penrose transformation to all solutions of the twistor equation, including the general case of non-self-dual solutions. Furthermore, we examine the properties of the resulting objects in spin cohomology, an $Ext$-space in the representation ring of $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ that arises from the adjoint of the tangent bundle of twistor space.

We're proposing innovative methods for underground mapping using muons.  Muons, being easily affected by the Earth's gravitational field, change direction in a manner that's directly related to the gravitational field's local gradient.  A detector can track these changes in momentum by measuring the time difference between the arrival of a muon event at the surface and its detection by an underground sensor, taking into account the Earth's rotation for more accurate timing.  Furthermore, we suggest an approach for spatially locating the source of the muons within the underground structure.  A simulation-based evaluation of the effectiveness of this method has been conducted.  Lastly, we're exploring the potential for imaging underground tunnels with this technique.

A parsing expression parser relies on a recognition expression to determine its behavior, similar to top-down parsers that use a production-accepting non-terminal. This research explores how to enhance the GLL algorithm, originally proposed by Allen H. Goodman and Lei Li, who in 2001 showed its equivalent status to LL parsing. The study examines GLL parsing in relation to context-free grammars and its distinction from LL parsing, considering how various factors impact parsing time, including ambiguity, lookahead, and precomputing. The findings indicate that the GLL algorithm can achieve significant performance improvements by analyzing parsing paths and reducing backtracking.

We calculate the rate of vacuum Cherenkov radiation emanating from a charged particle in both a $U(1)$ symmetric and Higgs-inverted type A model at a finite temperature. The temperature impact is such that the Cherenkov radiation rate increases as the temperature rises, with this increase being more pronounced in models with a larger Higgs field value.

To better understand language processing, researchers have been studying the role of prediction in typical utterance structures. Existing methods for analyzing prediction are limited to using fully trained neural language models, but this approach comes with several drawbacks, including a narrow scope of focus and a specific set of stimuli. Furthermore, these models do not natively support the tracking of linguistic predictions. To address these issues, we have developed an innovative approach that employs neural language models to dynamically update and refine predictions in real-time. This approach is applied to the analysis of a large dataset of spoken German and a set of German neural language models. Our results not only replicate previous findings on language processing but also reveal new insights into the role of linguistic structure in predicting utterance outcomes.

A novel, straightforward method for determining the three-dimensional form of unknown objects has been developed. The method relies on a dataset comprising objects that have been turned by hand. Given that objects viewed from different angles will also exhibit different turntables, it's possible to deduce their three-dimensional form. The challenge lies in identifying which objects correspond to the most relevant views and in determining the rotation matrices that describe these views. The new method identifies the relevant turntables by measuring the similarity between the views of the unknown object and the turntables in the database. The similarity is measured by applying a geometric transformation to the turntables and assessing the resulting alignment. The method has been tested using a dataset of objects viewed from a single side, and it has been found to achieve results comparable to those of a more complex deep learning model. The new method's ease of use is attributed to the use of hand-crafted features and simple algorithms, which makes it easier to understand and understandable.

Our research focuses on the control of Andreev bound states in a quantum dot connected to superconducting and normal metal electrodes via quantum point contacts. By adjusting the electrode geometry, the behavior of ABCR and ECT can be controlled, and we have found that these processes are significantly influenced by the presence of ABCR-induced AB states. Specifically, when an AB state is present, the conductance through an adjacent ECT channel is greatly reduced, and when a particular electron is removed from the superconductor, the conductance gap associated with ABCR splits into two distinct parts. This double peak is caused by the interaction between ABCR-induced AB states and the ABCR process itself.

The acceleration of particles in magnetic reconnection is studied through a one-dimensional, time-dependent kinetic model. The simulation incorporates a random, position-dependent change in velocity direction, and the results are compared to simulations that account for such changes and those that assume a uniform change for all particles. The inclusion of velocity changes leads to significantly higher particle energy levels in non-accelerated regions of space. Additionally, the results show that magnetic reconnection occurs at a lower rate when velocity changes are included. The simulation reveals distinct differences in particle energy distribution depending on whether velocity changes are accounted for, and it suggests that neglecting velocity changes may result in an underestimation of hot, non-thermal electrons associated with reconnected magnetic fields.

We investigate the impact of extended scalar sectors on precision measurements of the Higgs boson and two photons in electron-positron collisions. By focusing on the simplest extension of the Standard Model, the SM3 model, our analysis reveals that the model's parameter space can be tightly constrained using the observed value of the Higgs mass at the LHC. Subsequently, we use these constraints to assess the sensitivity of future electron-positron colliders in probing the SM3 parameter space through the electron-positron to Higgs plus photons process.
A formula for the subdifferential of the joint numerical radius is developed and utilized to investigate the best approximation problems associated with this quantity.

The widespread adoption of the Internet has led to the rapid growth of e-commerce and financial services, which has significantly improved people's daily lives but also raised concerns about data security. To mitigate these concerns, researchers have focused on differential privacy, a widely accepted framework for protecting personal data. However, previous studies primarily concentrated on traditional e-commerce services, neglecting the needs of financial services. To bridge this gap, this paper proposes a novel financial differential privacy framework, comprising three key components: financial privacy models, privacy-preserving mechanisms, and a quantitative analysis of the effects of differential privacy on financial services. The results show that our framework can provide satisfactory utility while ensuring robust security for financial services. The feasibility of the proposed framework is also demonstrated through a practical application example.

This research paper examines a novel approach to defining stochastic processes and stochastic fields, focusing on the correlation approach. In this study, we define a stochastic process or field by identifying the correlation kernel, which is the integral transform of the covariance function. This approach has several benefits, including its compatibility with Wiener measure and the preservation of positive semi-definiteness in covariance kernels. Building upon this concept, we define a random measure on a measurable space and a random function on a topological field, utilizing the correlation kernel. A key aspect of this work is the derivation of a method for finding the correlation kernel of a given stochastic field. Furthermore, we provide alternative definitions of a stochastic process or field, including the correlation kernel of a stationary process, the correlation kernel of a Gaussian process, and the correlation kernel of a stationary random measure.

Researchers achieved reliable ignition of high-pressure hydrogen-oxygen mixtures, diluted with helium, using a laser pump even when the laser beam was not precisely focused. In experiments conducted at pressures between 0.1 and 500 bar, using He, H2, and O2 gases, they discovered that the hydrogen-oxygen mixtures became ignitable at a critical energy obtained from simulations of laser absorption in gases. These simulations took into account both thermal and chemical absorption effects. In particular, they discovered that at lower pressures, the hydrogen-oxygen mixtures ignited reliably when the thermal and chemical absorption rates of energy were comparable, while at higher pressures, they observed a similar phenomenon but with an additional effect of chemical reactions occurring more rapidly in gas phase zones. In this case, the energy from absorption was transferred to the flame front, allowing ignition to occur. In experiments, they found that the energy threshold for reliable ignition agreed with the predictions of absorption simulations, and they discovered that the ignition delay times of gas mixtures fell within a certain range, increasing with pressure.

Deep learning-based segmentation frameworks are becoming increasingly adopted in mobile and web development, leveraging real-time image analysis. Although numerous segmentation models have been proposed, most require fixed training data and specific applications, while others rely on a time-consuming, user-driven process, including a manual input of boundaries. In this study, a novel boundary-aware segmentation framework is introduced, capable of achieving high accuracy and handling diverse tasks, including image segmentation, object detection, and saliency mapping, without the need for retraining. The framework is designed to be lightweight and cross-platform, suitable for mobile and web development, without compromising performance. The proposed method is evaluated on three datasets: PASCAL VOC, MS COCO, and DUTS-TR, demonstrating its ability to outperform competing models and provide superior boundary accuracy. The framework is open-sourced and accessible via GitHub.

Autonomous vehicles rely heavily on sensor data, which isn't sufficient for handling complex situations like lane changes and mergers. To overcome this limitation, cooperative driving techniques that utilize wireless communication among nearby vehicles are being explored. A key component of these systems is the beacon message, which is transmitted at regular intervals. However, generating these messages requires a delicate balance between their frequency and the information they contain. This research proposes a method for designing beacon messages that maximize their utility by incorporating context-specific information, such as the intentions of nearby vehicles and road conditions. A novel system is presented, which is comprised of three modules: one for extracting vital data from video feeds, another for processing and analyzing the data in real-time, and a third for generating the beacon messages. The system's performance is evaluated using a dataset collected from the 3D game, Unity3D, and the results show significant improvements in lane change assistance applications.

This research focuses on understanding how boundaries affect non-interacting particles moving passively in confined environments. We've identified a way to calculate the effective temperature of these particles based on the hydrodynamic temperature using a specific, dimensionless value called the boundary parameter, which depends on the boundary's reflectivity and the cross-sectional area. By studying this boundary parameter, we've discovered that it has a direct relationship with the particle's diffusion coefficient and drift speed, and it also influences the time it takes for the particle to settle down when still. We've applied our findings to a specific, two-dimensional scenario involving a disk with different shapes and found that the disk's thickness has a significant impact on these properties.

The average atom method is a technique used to model highly excited states in a system with a saturated and coupled nuclear fuel. It has been proven effective in certain scenarios, but there are situations where it falls short. Specifically, in cases where the continuum and bound states are tightly coupled, such as during nuclear reactions, the method tends to underestimate the energy differences between these states. This inaccuracy is attributed to the complex interactions within the atom's inner shell. To address this issue, a new variant of the average atom method is being developed, which incorporates the energy of Siegert states - a type of state that is analogous to bound states. By doing so, the method aims to more accurately capture the interactions within the atom's inner shell. This version of the average atom method has been applied to the nuclear data of uranium isotopes and the results indicate a significant improvement in the energy spectrum of the atom. Additionally, the method has been shown to provide a more accurate estimate of the inner shell binding energy, bringing it in line with the results of more advanced relativistic mean-field models.

Observations of the Si IV 1390-6 nm doublet in a solar flare were made using the International Space Station's IRIS, which allowed for extremely high-resolution and cadence studies. The resulting data revealed rapid changes in emission intensity across the 81.5 arcsecond wide by 225 arcsecond wide observation area at a 1.2 second cadence. A notable correlation existed between the Si IV 1390-6 line intensities, although this correlation was more pronounced in the blue-shifted component. A distinct blue peak in the line profiles, which appeared at the 4.4% level of the red line, correlated with the blue-shifted component. A similar correlation was found between the blue peak and line centre variations. A strong correlation existed between the Si IV 1390-6 line intensities and intensities of other spectral lines, such as He I 584.2 nm, He II 256.3 nm, and C IV 1548-86 nm. A model was proposed to explain the observed correlation, which suggested that the observed variations were caused by the excitation of resonant Lyman-alpha lines by non-thermal electrons. A comparison of the calculated and observed Si IV 1390-6 line intensities indicated that the non-thermal electron flux was approximately 10^9 part cm^2 part s^-1, which was consistent with the observed variations of the He I 584.2 nm and C IV 154

A solution to the strong CP issue necessitates the existence of an almost undetectable pseudoscalar particle, the axion, in our universe. The axion's cosmological destiny, however, is contingent upon its mass, which must be minimal in order to resolve the CP issue, yet substantial in order to have a viable cosmological impact. The mass of the axion being greater than about $10^{-5}$ eV would result in an axion that decays before the present time, preventing it from acting as a dark matter candidate. The mass of the axion being less than about $10^{-6}$ eV would result in an axion that has not yet decayed and could potentially serve as dark matter, despite still being undetectable. The mass of the axion being between these two values would lead to an axion that has not yet had a chance to decay but which is not a suitable dark matter candidate. The mass of the axion being greater than about $10^{-6}$ eV would result in an axion that has not had a chance to decay, but which is not a suitable dark matter candidate. The mass of the axion being greater than about $10^{4}$ eV would result in an axion that has already decayed into dark matter, in a scenario where dark matter is composed of ordinary axions. The impact of the angular distribution of particles emitted during ion irradiation on the formation of nano-scale patterns is investigated, with a focus on how this distribution influences the optimal angle for pattern creation. Building on a previous study, this research examines the relationship between material properties and irradiation conditions, particularly as they relate to the physical factors contributing to this phenomenon.
